title: Integrated Transcriptome-Metabolome Analysis of Rps2-A226Y Mutant Liver
text: Mammalian liver coordinates glucose, lipid and amino-acid metabolism, which makes it a sensible tissue for asking how a body-wide proteostatic stress shows up in metabolism. This post looks at liver transcriptomics and metabolomics from female Rps2-A226Y knock-in mice, which carry a ribosomal ambiguity mutation that increases missense mistranslation, compared with Cre-expressing wild-type controls. The mutant allele is expressed mosaically, and the mutant transcript accounts for roughly a quarter of liver Rps2 mRNA, so effect sizes should be read as diluted relative to the full mutant effect. Sample ages are reported as recorded in the metadata and are being checked against the animal records. This analysis is my part of a PhD project carried out between 2020 and 2022.

title: Integrated Transcriptome-Metabolome Analysis of Rps2-A226Y Mutant Liver
text:
Why This Analysis
This post summarizes an integrated liver omics analysis in female mice carrying Rps2-A226Y, comparing mutant versus wildtype at two corrected ages: 9 months and 15 months.
The workflow combines differential transcriptomics and metabolomics to identify pathway-level progression across time, with emphasis on bile acid metabolism, oxidative stress, lipid remodeling, and protein quality control pathways.

title: Integrated Transcriptome-Metabolome Analysis of Rps2-A226Y Mutant Liver
text:
Main Biological Takeaways

The mutant phenotype is progressive from 9m to 15m across both omics layers.
Bile acid pathway dysregulation strengthens with age and remains a dominant signature.
Stress-adaptation programs appear stronger earlier, with altered regulatory balance later.
Lipid and antioxidant pathway changes support age-dependent metabolic remodeling.
Most strongly significant features preserve direction across time, with selective switches.
Sphingomyelin species accumulate broadly, consistent with a chain-length-dependent ceramide synthase (Cers2/Cers4) shift toward the SM-conversion arm of the pathway.
Lysosomal genes, especially cathepsins, are broadly downregulated alongside XIAP upregulation, consistent with a lysosome-linked anti-apoptotic adaptation.
Pre-ranked GSEA (fgsea + MSigDB) independently recovers bile acid metabolism and proteasome/protein-degradation signatures among the top pathways.
Gene-metabolite concordance is not uniform across pathways: some (amino acid, purine/pyrimidine) agree in direction, while bile acid and lipid pathways show more disagreement worth further investigation.
A database-driven enrichment cross-check (SMPDB via MetaboAnalystR) is only weakly informative here: roughly 20% of measured metabolites appear in SMPDB, and that subset is biased against lipids. Correcting the statistical background from the pathway library to the measured metabolome weakens every contrast by about an order of magnitude, leaving no FDR-significant pathway at either age.
What remains is a nominal, uncorrected tendency toward depletion of TCA-adjacent intermediates and carnitine at 9 months, driven by a small overlapping metabolite set.

title: Mounting the Beast: A DIY Guide to Installing a Beastmaker 1000 Hangboard
text:
Every climber reaches a point in their journey where they look at the empty space above their bedroom door and think: “I could put a hangboard there.”
This is the story of how that thought became a reality, turning a blank wall into a finger-strength training station. Here is the step-by-step saga of mounting a Beastmaker 1000 Series hangboard above a concrete door frame.


Step 1: The Blank Canvas
It all starts with a dream and a blank wall. The space above a doorway is ideal because it allows your legs and body to hang freely, but it is also a high-stress area. You cannot simply screw a hangboard directly into the plaster; you need a solid plan to anchor it safely.



The empty wall above the doorway—full of potential, but currently blank.





Step 2: The Foundation (Metolius Backing Board)
To avoid tearing down the wall and to distribute the forces evenly, we use a wooden backing board (in this case, a Metolius mounting board). This board is anchored securely into the solid wall structure, providing a stable, flat surface to screw the Beastmaker into.



The pre-drilled Metolius backing board, waiting to bridge the gap between the wall and the hangboard.





Step 3: Unboxing the Beast & Preparing the Power
With the backing board ready, it was time to open the main event: the Beastmaker 1000. Alongside the beautiful wooden board, I dug out my trusty Texmash TDU-1000 impact drill. A solid drill is non-negotiable when dealing with concrete or brick walls.



Unboxing the Beastmaker and prepping the Texmash TDU-1000 drill.





Step 4: Organizing the Arsenal
DIY projects live and die by preparation. I gathered the essential tools for the job: * A LUX-TOOLS 40 cm spirit level (crucial—nobody wants to train on a slanted board). * A utility knife for opening packages and clean cuts. * A masonry drill bit matching the anchor size. * A screwdriver and selection of screws.



Gathering the essential tools for a precise installation.





Step 5: Choosing the Right Anchors
When hanging your body weight (plus dynamic force) off a wall, cheap drywall screws won’t cut it. I opted for Fischer S 8x40 wall plugs (8mm diameter, 40mm depth) and matching heavy-duty black wood screws.

[!TIP] Always check the packaging recommendations. For the Fischer S 8x40, a hole depth of at least 50mm and an 8mm drill bit are required for maximum load capacity.




Fischer S 8x40 wall plugs and heavy-duty screws—the unsung heroes of this project.





Step 6: Making the Holes
With the backing board held up and leveled, I marked the drilling points. Then came the noisy, messy part: drilling the 12 anchor holes. You can see the neat little piles of concrete dust resting on top of the door frame, a testament to the Texmash’s impact mode.



Twelve clean holes drilled above the door frame. Measure twice, drill once!





Step 7: Inserting Anchors & Preparing Screws
Next, the Fischer wall plugs were tapped into the holes, and the long black screws were started. Having the screws partially inserted in the wall beforehand makes aligning and mounting the heavy wooden backing board much easier.



The screws aligned and ready to catch the backing board.





Step 8: Securing the Backing Board
The backing board is up! It went on smoothly and was screwed tight until it was completely flush with the wall. A quick check with the spirit level confirmed everything was perfectly horizontal.



The Metolius backing board is securely mounted and leveled.





Step 9: Unleashing the Beastmaker
Finally, the moment of truth. The Beastmaker 1000 was aligned on the backing board and screwed in using the wood screws provided. The wood-on-wood mount is incredibly strong and looks fantastic.



The finished setup: The Beastmaker 1000 is ready for training.


With the board solid as a rock, it was time to chalk up and test the 35-degree slopers. Let the training sessions begin!

        Biography

        I am a Discovery Postdoc in computational and systems biology at Novartis Biomedical Research in Basel, Switzerland. In my current work, I apply bulk and single-cell RNA-seq alongside SomaScan proteomics to correlate molecular profiles with clinical outcomes. I collaborate closely with multidisciplinary teams to investigate the mechanisms and biomarkers of tendinopathy, osteoarthritis, and tissue regeneration using statistical modeling, machine learning, and bioimaging approaches.

        Previously, I was a Postdoctoral Researcher in the Department of Biomedicine at the University of Basel / University Hospital Basel (2023–2024), where I studied the gut-liver axis in Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease (MASLD), performing scRNA-seq analyses of mucosal-associated innate-like T cells, multivariate modeling of patient microbiota dynamics, and bioimage quantification of intestinal barrier integrity. I earned my Ph.D. in Cell and Systems Biology at the University of Zurich (2017–2022) in the group of Prof. Erik C. Böttger, investigating how ribosomal mistranslation shapes proteostasis, ER stress, and mitochondrial function via transcriptomics, metabolomics, and fluorescence microscopy.

        My core passion is transforming complex clinical and biological data into actionable insights through exploratory data analysis, rigorous hypothesis testing, and interactive data visualization (R/Bioconductor, Python, UNIX/HPC, Quarto, Shiny). title: A Knowledge Base for One Decision: Helping My Mother Choose an AMD Treatment
text:
My mother has age-related macular degeneration (AMD). Sooner or later, the conversation with her ophthalmologist will come down to a choice between two injected drugs: Vabysmo (faricimab) and Eylea (aflibercept). Both are given as injections into the eye, often for years, so the choice matters: it decides how often she has to come in for an injection, and how well the disease stays under control between visits.
I didn’t want to walk into that appointment knowing only the brand names. So I built a small website, the Macula Disease Knowledge Base, that collects what the clinical trials and recent reviews actually say, with every fact traced back to its source. It isn’t meant to replace her doctor. It’s meant to help us ask better questions.


The site
Here it is, live. You can browse it right inside this post, or open it in a new tab.

  


  The embedded site opens in its light theme; the toggle in its top-right corner switches to dark or to a Russian interface.

It has four parts:

Clinical trials: plain-language digests of the pivotal trials comparing faricimab with aflibercept: TENAYA & LUCERNE in wet AMD, and YOSEMITE & RHINE in diabetic macular oedema. Each card covers the design, the treatment arms, the exact posted outcomes and the safety.
Knowledge check: how AMD works and progresses, explained in layers from basic to molecular. It has hand-drawn diagrams of the eye and of the VEGF / Ang-2 signalling that these drugs target, plus self-check questions, in English and Russian.
Wiki: the core of the project. There are 43 pages on diseases, mechanisms, drugs and trials, and every statement cites the paper it came from.
Wiki map: a 3-D graph of how all those pages connect. Click any node to read the page.




The wiki page that matters most for us: what the evidence says about Vabysmo versus Eylea 2 mg and 8 mg, with a source citation after every claim.





The knowledge check in Russian, starting from an annotated diagram of the eye that shows where the macula is.





The wiki map: one node per page, sized by how many pages link to it and coloured by type (ideas, things, sources).





How it’s built
I built it together with an AI coding assistant (Claude Code), but with strict rules about where knowledge is allowed to come from:

Sources go into a raw/ folder and are never edited. So far these are four recent open-access reviews (2024–2026): a broad clinical update, a review of the molecular mechanisms, a review of therapeutic options, and a perspective comparing faricimab with high-dose aflibercept.
The wiki is written from those sources only. Each page covers one idea, drug or trial, and every factual sentence ends with a citation to the source file it came from. When the assistant combines several sources into its own conclusion, that’s explicitly labelled as synthesis.
Contradictions are kept, not smoothed over. When two sources disagree, both claims stay on the page side by side. For example, one review credits omega-3 fatty acids for the 25% benefit of the AREDS2 eye vitamins, while another describes the formula with no omega-3 at all. These disagreements turned out to be some of the most useful findings, because they show exactly which numbers to double-check.
Open questions go into a research task list, to be answered later with new sources.

One command regenerates the website’s wiki and the 3-D map after every update. The whole site is static files hosted for free on GitHub Pages, and the source is on GitHub. I’ve since turned the setup into a reusable template, so I can start the same kind of knowledge base on any other topic in a minute.



What I’ve learned so far
From the evidence collected so far (summarised on the site’s decision page):

Both newer options keep vision as well as standard Eylea. In the TENAYA & LUCERNE trials, Vabysmo given up to every 16 weeks was non-inferior to Eylea 2 mg every 8 weeks. In the PULSAR trial, high-dose Eylea 8 mg given every 12 or 16 weeks was too.
The realistic gain is fewer injections, not better vision. About 45% of patients on Vabysmo were already on 16-week intervals after the first year.
Fewer injections matters in real life. Outside trials, patients often get fewer injections than they need, and vision suffers. Reviews call this the “durability gap”.
There’s no head-to-head trial of Vabysmo versus Eylea 8 mg. Both were tested against the same comparator, but never against each other, so any comparison between them is indirect.
The extra mechanism isn’t proven to matter yet. Vabysmo also blocks angiopoietin-2, which should stabilise blood vessels. But a phase 2 trial found no clear benefit from that part, and its longer intervals may partly come from the dose.
Safety looked similar in the trials. Neither drug caused more eye inflammation than standard Eylea.



Questions we’ll take to the ophthalmologist

How often would each option need to be injected for her, and how is the interval adjusted?
Which drugs are available and covered here, including Eylea 8 mg?
If fluid persists on one drug, is switching to the other an option?
What signs at home (e.g. on an Amsler grid) should prompt an earlier visit?




What’s next
The site’s task list already has the next questions: long-term (3-year) results and any head-to-head comparisons, real-world safety data since approval, and what happens when patients switch drugs. As I add sources, the wiki, the map and the site update together.
This is a family project to understand the evidence. It isn’t medical advice, and every treatment decision belongs with her ophthalmologist.
